title: Broadway Review: PUNCH - Bored and Confused?
transcript: Hello and welcome to Bored and Confused, where I review shows based on two criteria. One, was I bored? Two, was I confused. Today's show is Punch, playing at Manhattan Theater Club's Freriedman Theater. Now, before I get into it, please remember to like, comment, and subscribe. It really helps me grow this channel which allows me to see more theater and make more of these videos so that we can talk about everything that's going on in the world of New York theater. Now, Punch is written by James Graham and based on the book Right from Wrong by Jacob Dunn and it's directed by Adam Penford. So, what is Punch about? Punch tells the true story of Jacob Dunn, a young man whose single impulsive act of violence changes multiple lives forever. The play follows Jacob as he recounts his past to a restorative justice circle, a sort of group therapy. He explores the events that led to a tragic death and the consequences that ripple outward. Through these reflections, the audience witnesses his anger, confusion, and gradual reckoning, as well as the impact on the victim's family as well as his own. The story examines themes of accountability, redemption, and the human capacity for change, balancing the darkness of the incident with moments of hope, empathy, and emotional catharsis. So, a little background on the play. This play premiered at Noddingham Playhouse, which is where the real life events that inspired the story actually took place. It then had a run at the Old Vic in London and now it's heading to the West End for a strictly limited 10-week engagement at the Apollo Theater from September 22nd till November 29th. Interesting how the Broadway run and the West End run are overlapping each other. So, was I bored? Was I confused? Nope. Not bored or confused. This is a tight two-act play that moves efficiently. The story is very clear. Each of the lead actors plays two roles, some more, and the small ensemble supports these shifts seamlessly. Ideally, I'd have liked a bigger cast so that everyone could stick to a single role, but the doubling works well enough here, and the skilled direction and the performances never leave you confused. Quick costume changes are a factor, but they pull it off impressively. The first act of this play is very dark. It's heavy and sad, and it spends a lot of time establishing Jacob's situation and his anger, which makes the exposition feel a little dense at times. Part of that is the storytelling approach, though, because Jacob is speaking directly to his therapy circle, explaining what happened, but at times it can feel a little bit like a TED talk. But that's kind of part for the course for adaptations of these kind of narrative memoirs. I've seen other plays based on true stories use this device successfully and it still works theatrically. It gives the audience context. It adds moments of reflection and it even provides some breaks of humor or insight from Jacob's older self. But after an hour of Jacob's teenage angst and bad behavior, I was anxious to reach the moment of emotional breakthrough. The second act is unquestionably stronger. It's when we finally see the meeting between the victim's family and Jacob. the moment that the story has been building towards and emotionally it lands but it's not the kind of explosive all characters at the dinner table scene that some plays build tension towards. That said, the writing, direction, and performances carry the weight beautifully, making the second act much more dynamic and emotionally satisfying. Some of the storytelling can feel a little heavy-handed at times, almost like it's preaching to the choir, but I get why. For a younger audience or anyone who's new to these kind of stories, it may be necessary to drive the points home about consequences and to teach them about restorative justice. Now, the performances all around are excellent. Will Harrison is compelling as Jacob and Camila Konoflavia has a dual role playing both his love interest and the restorative justice facilitator, which she handles seamlessly. It was great to see these two on stage together again, having enjoyed their performances in the Coastal Starlight at the Mitsy New House Theater at Lincoln Center a few seasons back. Lucy Taylor is heartbreaking and nuanced as Jacob's struggling mother, and she's infectiously upbeat as Jacob's parole officer. Victoria Clark and Sam Roards are great as the big-hearted parents of the victim. Everyone on the stage is fully committed, and it really elevates the story and the heavy subject matter. This is good theater. It's well written. It's well directed and it's well performed. Now, the first act is dark and heavy, but the second act brings emotional payoff and hope. While it may feel like a PSA at times, it's a story worth seeing. If the subject matter interests you or if you want to see these talented Broadway actors in action, definitely make your way over to the Samuel J. Freriedman Theater for Punch. And talking about the Freriedman, it is one of my favorite houses. It's very intimate with a mezzanine that has a great rake, so everyone has a really good view of the stage.
